system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2131-06-26 16:17:00 to 2131-06-27 15:08:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for his tenth cycle of high-dose methotrexate since CNS lymphoma relapse, marking the sixth maintenance dose and third bimonthly administration. He tolerated the chemotherapy infusion well without complications. His candidal chest rash continued to improve, and he remained neurologically stable with no new deficits. Methotrexate levels were monitored and cleared appropriately, reaching 0.06 before discharge. Liver enzymes rose transiently as expected. Aspirin, omeprazole, and fluconazole were held during treatment and restarted at discharge. A brain MRI showed no new enhancing lesions, indicating stable disease. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up scheduled in three months.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CT HEAD W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ with dizziness, history of CNS lymphoma  // Eval for bleed

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial images from skullbase to vertex were obtained
without intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformats were also
performed.

DOSE:   This study involved 3 CT acquisition phases with dose indices as
follows:
   1) CT Localizer Radiograph
   2) CT Localizer Radiograph
   3) Sequenced Acquisition 16.0 s, 16.4 cm; CTDIvol = 48.9 mGy (Head) DLP =
802.7 mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Head) = 803 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  MR head ___

FINDINGS: 

There is no evidence of acute territorial infarction or hemorrhage. Left
posterior limb of the internal capsule hypodensity extending into the left
cerebral peduncle is again noted, and corresponds to the abnormalities seen on
FLAIR sequence on recent MRI.  Focal white matter hypodensity in the left
frontal centrum semiovale (02:22) is nonspecific, but may be due to chronic
small vessel ischemic disease.  Mild prominence of the ventricles and sulci is
suggestive of age-appropriate involutional changes.

Left frontal burr hole is again seen.  Mucosal thickening in the left
maxillary sinus is minimal.  There is mild mucosal thickening in the ethmoid
air cells, sphenoid sinuses, and left frontoethmoidal recess.  The mastoid air
cells and middle ear cavities are clear. The orbits are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:


1. No acute intracranial hemorrhage or new mass effect.
2. Hypodensity within the posterior limb of the left internal capsule
extending into the left cerebral peduncle appears similar to the signal
abnormalities seen on prior MRI and are better assessed on that modality.  No
new gross lesions are identified on this CT exam, but MRI with contrast is a
more sensitive study.

EXAMINATION:  MR HEAD W AND W/O CONTRAST T9112 MR HEAD

INDICATION:  ___ w/ CNS lymphoma (dx ___, recurred ___ as well as h/o
composite Hodgkin's and non-Hodkin's lymphoma dx in ___ s/p ABVD, rituximab,
and mBACOD w/ complete systemic response who developed CNS-only relapse now in
remission after starting reinduction HDMTX who presents with a sensation of
something moving in his head.  // Evaluate for progression of his CNS
lymphoma.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal and axial T1 weighted imaging were performed. After
administration of 8 mL of Gadavist intravenous contrast, axial imaging was
performed with gradient echo, FLAIR, diffusion, and T1 technique. Sagittal
MPRAGE imaging was performed and re-formatted in axial and coronal
orientations.

COMPARISON:  Head CT ___ and brain MR ___.

FINDINGS: 

There is no evidence of hemorrhage, edema, masses, mass effect, midline shift
or recent infarction.  Again seen are areas of white matter hyperintensity on
FLAIR that most likely represent chronic small vessel ischemia.  A tract of
hyperintensity extending into the left cerebral peduncle may reflect Wallerian
degeneration.  The ventricles and sulci are prominent in an atrophic pattern. 
There is no abnormal enhancement after contrast administration.

IMPRESSION:


1. No change since ___.  White matter changes likely reflecting
chronic ischemia.  No evidence of hemorrhage or recent infarction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Reyes, one of the neurology team. I understand you've been feeling a strange sensation in your head—like something moving. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. It’s not pain, exactly—more like a crawling or shifting feeling inside, mostly on the left side. I thought it might be dizziness at first, but it’s different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of CNS lymphoma and the relapse last year, we want to make sure this isn’t related to any new activity in the brain. You’ve had chemotherapy, including high-dose methotrexate—how have you been feeling overall since your last treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired, but that’s normal for me now. No new headaches or weakness. The rash on my chest has been better since I restarted the fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from this morning—it showed no bleeding or new mass. But because MRI is more sensitive for detecting lymphoma changes, we’ve scheduled a contrast-enhanced brain MRI for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the MRI tell us for sure if the cancer is back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s our best tool right now. It can show if there’s any new tumor growth or inflammation. The fact that you’re not having other neurological symptoms—like vision changes, weakness, or seizures—is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just worried it’s coming back. Last time it was so sudden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. But remember, your last MRI three months ago showed stable disease, and your methotrexate levels were clearing well. We’re being cautious by checking now, not because we expect the worst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about the feeling in my head? Could it be from the old damage in my brain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The area of scarring in your left internal capsule and cerebral peduncle could cause unusual sensations. Sometimes the brain misinterprets signals from damaged areas. But we won’t know for sure until we see the MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI results are back. I’m happy to tell you there’s no evidence of new tumor, bleeding, or abnormal enhancement. The findings are unchanged from your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not the lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, there’s no sign of progression. The white matter changes we see are consistent with chronic small vessel disease and old scarring—likely from prior treatment. The sensation you’re feeling may be related to that, or possibly even benign nerve signaling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this afternoon. We’ll make sure your primary oncologist knows about this episode. You should continue your current medications, including fluconazole for the candidiasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more chemo this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your treatment schedule remains as planned. We’ll follow up with your oncology team to confirm your next methotrexate dose in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge paperwork is ready. We’re documenting the sensation in your head as a transient neurological symptom, likely non-progressive given the normal MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I was really anxious about this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll make sure you have a follow-up appointment with neurology in four weeks, and your oncologist will see you in three months. Call us sooner if the sensation returns or if you develop any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll get the discharge order processed, and you should be able to leave by early afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check-in before you go. All your labs are stable, and the nursing team confirms you’re feeling well. Here’s your discharge summary and medication list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll make sure to keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care of yourself, Mr. Thompson. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted following a report of a sensation of movement in his head, raising concern for possible CNS lymphoma progression. He has a history of composite Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma with CNS relapse, previously treated with high-dose methotrexate. A non-contrast CT head showed no acute hemorrhage or mass effect. A subsequent MRI with contrast revealed no new enhancing lesions, hemorrhage, or edema, indicating stable disease. His symptoms were likely related to chronic brain changes from prior illness or treatment. He remained neurologically stable throughout admission, with no interventions required. He was discharged home with follow-up planned in neurology and oncology clinics.
